title: Chelsea's New Era: Clearlake Takes Full Control as Boehly Exits
summary:
Chelsea, one of England's biggest soccer clubs, has a new boss — and it's not a person. On Wednesday, the club announced that Clearlake Capital, a private equity company, would acquire the stakes of Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter. Clearlake, led by co-founders Behdad Eghbali and Jose E Feliciano, now has full control. Boehly's chairmanship is over.

Boehly and Walter are US billionaires who also co-own the Los Angeles Dodgers baseball team. They partnered with Clearlake to buy Chelsea from Roman Abramovich in May 2022, in a sale mandated by the British government. Before the new deal, Clearlake owned 61.5 percent. The Financial Times reported the pair would receive 950 million pounds ($1.27 billion) for their combined stakes, valuing the club at about five billion pounds including debt. Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss remains an important stakeholder.

On Thursday, Chelsea's new coach, Xabi Alonso, told reporters it was "an important day for the club." Alonso, who started on July 1, said he has "very good relations" with Eghbali. "He was the one that came to Madrid to explain to me the project, to convince me," Alonso said. The club's statement was direct: "Our ambition is clear: to compete at the highest level, to win major trophies, and to build sustained success."

That ambition is needed. Since the 2022 takeover, Chelsea's best Premier League finish is fourth in 2024/25, when they won the UEFA Conference League and FIFA Club World Cup. Last season, they finished a dismal 10th. This season, they have seven points from four games and sit sixth. Alonso, a former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen coach, has a brief to revitalize the squad. Boehly and Walter also sold their stakes in Chelsea's partner club, French side Strasbourg, giving Clearlake full control there too.
why_it_matters: Global finance increasingly shapes the sports teenagers follow: clubs become assets inside investment portfolios, and decisions about transfers, ticket prices, and multi-club networks follow the money rather than the fans.

background_read: Clearlake Capital is a private equity firm (a company that pools investors' money to buy large stakes in businesses, often aiming to sell them later at a profit) co-founded by Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano.
Chelsea is a west London club founded in 1905 that plays in the Premier League, the top division of English soccer and one of the most-watched sports leagues in the world.

Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich bought Chelsea in 2003 and bankrolled an era of trophies, including the club's first Champions League title in 2012. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the British government sanctioned him and forced a sale, which the Boehly–Clearlake group won with a then-record bid of about £4.25 billion.

The original deal split control: Clearlake held the majority of the shares while Boehly ran the club as chairman, an arrangement that reportedly produced friction between the partners almost from the start.
Buying a club partly with borrowed money means owners answer to lenders and to investors expecting a return — one reason supporters track ownership news as closely as transfer news.

perspectives.description: Clearlake now has a single, clear line of authority instead of a divided boardroom, which supporters of the deal say speeds up decisions. Coach Xabi Alonso publicly welcomed it, noting Eghbali personally flew to Madrid to convince him of the project.

Many fans are wary of private equity ownership: debt, cost-cutting, and treating a club as a tradable asset rather than a community institution. They note the ownership group has now changed shape twice in three years while results on the pitch stayed uneven.

The deal fits a wider pattern of American and Gulf capital buying into European soccer and building multi-club groups — Chelsea and Strasbourg under one owner being the clearest example. Valuation near £5bn shows clubs are now priced like media and entertainment businesses, not just sports teams.

The real test is sporting: a sixth-place start and a fourth-place ceiling since 2022 leave Alonso and the new owners under pressure to deliver trophies. Longer term, questions remain about how debt and investor expectations will shape transfers and ticket pricing.
